content: 1. A large population-based study on iron and folic acid supplementation in pregnant women was conducted, highlighting barriers and enablers to its implementation. 2. The PRISMA statement provides guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses, ensuring standardized reporting. 3. Self-management of iron and folic acid supplementation during pre-pregnancy, pregnancy, and postnatal periods has been systematically reviewed to assess its effectiveness. 4. Global and regional estimates of preeclampsia and eclampsia have been systematically reviewed, emphasizing their significant impact on maternal and neonatal health. 5. The global burden of preeclampsia and eclampsia has been extensively studied, revealing their critical role in maternal morbidity and mortality. 6. The association between maternal preeclampsia and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in very-low-birth-weight infants has been investigated, showing a significant correlation. 7. Chronic hypertension in pregnancy and its outcomes have been systematically reviewed, providing insights into maternal and perinatal risks. 8. The impact of antihypertensive treatment on maternal and perinatal outcomes in pregnancies complicated by chronic hypertension has been systematically reviewed and analyzed. 9. Home blood pressure monitoring has been shown to improve hypertension control and overcome therapeutic inertia, as evidenced by systematic reviews and meta-analyses. 10. The role of home blood pressure monitoring in diagnosing and managing hypertension has been systematically reviewed, highlighting its clinical utility. 11. The effects of home blood pressure monitoring on medication adherence have been systematically reviewed, demonstrating its positive impact. 12. Comparisons between home and clinic blood pressure readings during pregnancy have been systematically reviewed, showing differences in measurement accuracy. 13. Home blood pressure monitoring during antenatal and postpartum periods has been systematically reviewed, emphasizing its feasibility and effectiveness. 14. The feasibility and acceptability of self-testing for proteinuria during pregnancy have been explored using mixed methods approaches. 15. Self-testing for proteinuria in pregnancy has been systematically reviewed and analyzed, showing its potential for early detection and management. 16. The use of smartphone-based urine testing applications among women in prenatal care has been evaluated for feasibility and acceptability. 17. Self-monitoring of blood glucose during pregnancy has been systematically reviewed, highlighting its role in managing hyperglycemia. 18. The use of smartphone-based, interactive blood glucose management systems in women with gestational diabetes mellitus has been assessed for user satisfaction and acceptability. 19. The management of gestational diabetes using smart mobile telemedicine has been explored, demonstrating its potential for improving outcomes. 20. Women's experiences with using smartphone applications to manage gestational diabetes mellitus have been studied in randomized controlled trials. 21. The lived experiences of pregnant women with gestational diabetes mellitus in self-monitoring blood glucose have been explored through phenomenological research. 22. The provision of free pregnancy test kits to community health workers has been shown to increase contraceptive distribution, as evidenced by impact evaluations. 23. The acceptability and feasibility of phone follow-up after early medical abortion have been evaluated in randomized controlled trials. 24. Self-assessment of early medical abortion outcomes has been compared with clinic follow-up in randomized controlled trials, demonstrating non-inferiority. 25. The acceptability and feasibility of phone follow-up with semi-quantitative urine pregnancy tests after medical abortion have been studied in various settings. 26. Self-collection of samples for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) has been recommended as part of WHO guidelines on self-care interventions. 27. Human papillomavirus (HPV) self-sampling has been recommended as part of cervical cancer screening, according to WHO guidelines. 28. Updated recommendations on HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, antiretroviral initiation, and monitoring have been published by WHO. 29. The distribution of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in pharmacies has been systematically reviewed, highlighting its potential for HIV prevention. 30. Pharmacist-led PrEP programs have been implemented in high HIV prevalence areas, demonstrating their effectiveness and feasibility. 31. High awareness and willingness to pay for PrEP among young adults in Western Kenya have been reported in population-based surveys. 32. Willingness to discuss and screen for PrEP in pharmacies among men who have sex with men has been studied, showing positive attitudes. 33. The feasibility and acceptability of self-administration of gender-affirming hormones have been systematically reviewed, providing insights into transgender health care. 34. The global impact of transgender health care has been explored, emphasizing the need for inclusive and accessible services. 35. The WHO package of essential noncommunicable disease (PEN) interventions for primary health care has been developed to address global health challenges.
